## Before the bench {.center}

### What you are about to measure

Two sensors, an NTC and a Pt1000, go into the same stirred bath at the same
instants.

By the end of the session you will know:

- how to fit a genuinely nonlinear calibration curve to each, as an ordinary
  linear least squares problem;
- which of the two gives better resolution, in **kelvin**, against this
  platform's own measured noise floor;
- how much your own excitation choice warms the sensor above the medium it is
  supposed to be measuring.

### The rule of the session

::: {.callout-important}
## A calibration curve is only as good as the reference it was checked against

Both sensors are read against the **same** reference-thermometer value at
each bath point. If the two fitted curves disagree, that is the sensors —
not two baths that were never quite at the same temperature.
:::

## At the bench {.center}

### What you will build

An NTC in a resistive divider, a Pt1000 in a bridge with an instrumentation
amplifier, both reading the same bath.

::: {.smaller}
| Point | Source |
|---|---|
| `cal-ice` | Crushed ice, distilled water |
| `cal-t20` … `cal-t80` | Five stirred-water temperatures |
| `selfheat-high` | The `t50` point again, both sensors at higher excitation |
:::

### Seven runs, seven sidecars

```bash
arduino-io mode 15 analog && arduino-io mode 16 analog
arduino-io stream 15,16 --hz 1000 --seconds 0.2 --csv data/cal-t50.csv
# ... re-wire nothing, re-read the reference thermometer, repeat
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two things that ruin the session

Read the reference thermometer **at each point**, not once at the start. And
record the excitation actually used on the self-heating run — without it,
$\delta$ cannot be recovered from the data at all.
:::

### Then

Open [the handbook](handbook.qmd) for the full procedure, and one of the two
analysis templates — [Python](analysis-py.qmd) or [R](analysis-r.qmd).

They have the same sections and produce the same numbers. Both ship with
reference data, so you can read the whole analysis before you wire anything.

## What you should come away with {.center}

### Three sentences you should be able to defend

1. "The NTC's Steinhart–Hart fit and the Pt1000's Callendar–Van Dusen fit are
   both ordinary linear least squares, because $\dots$"
2. "At $T = \dots\,^\circ$C, sensor $\dots$ gives a better temperature
   resolution, $\delta T_\mathrm{res} = \dots$ K, because its sensitivity of
   $\dots$ V/K divided by S1's noise floor of $\dots$ V is smaller than the
   other sensor's."
3. "Driving sensor $\dots$ harder shifted its apparent reading by $\dots$ K,
   consistent with a dissipation constant of $\dots$ mW/K."

If you can say those three with your own numbers in them, the session worked.
